claim: Monkeys viewed two sequentially presented stimuli on each trial: an unoccluded shape (reference) and either an unoccluded or a partially occluded shape (test).
source: On each trial, monkeys viewed two sequentially presented stimuli: an unoccluded shape (reference) and either an unoccluded or a partially occluded shape (test).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental task design presented in the manuscript text.

claim: Monkeys reported whether the two shapes were the same or different by making a saccade to the right or left choice target, respectively.
source: Monkeys reported whether the two shapes were the same or different by making a saccade to the right or left choice target, respectively.
evidence: This describes the behavioral response method used in the experimental task.

claim: Monkey performance was near 100% for unoccluded stimuli (100% visible area).
source: Performance was near 100% for unoccluded stimuli (100% visible area) and declined gradually for higher occlusion levels (i.e. <100% visible area).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: Monkey performance declined gradually for higher occlusion levels.
source: Performance was near 100% for unoccluded stimuli (100% visible area) and declined gradually for higher occlusion levels (i.e. <100% visible area).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: Many vlPFC neurons responded strongly to occluded stimuli and weakly to unoccluded stimuli.
source: Many neurons responded strongly to occluded stimuli and weakly to unoccluded stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement of neurophysiological observations from vlPFC recordings.

claim: For vlPFC example neuron 1, responses were stronger when the shapes were occluded (colored lines) than unoccluded (black lines).
source: For both the preferred and non-preferred shape, responses were stronger when the shapes were occluded (colored lines) than unoccluded (black lines).
evidence: This describes the response pattern shown in Figure 2A-B for an example vlPFC neuron.

claim: vlPFC example neuron 1 responses were more discriminable when the shapes were occluded.
source: These responses were also more discriminable when the shapes were occluded: shape selectivity was stronger for occluded than unoccluded stimuli (Figure 2C; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes shape selectivity analysis shown in Figure 2C for an example vlPFC neuron.

claim: vlPFC example neuron 2 showed no preference for either of the two shapes used.
source: However, this neuron showed no preference for either of the two shapes used; shape selectivity was therefore weak for occluded and unoccluded stimuli (Figure 2F).
evidence: This describes the lack of shape selectivity for a second example vlPFC neuron shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Most vlPFC neurons (71/98) had negative slopes in the regression between % visible area and average responses, indicating stronger responses to occluded stimuli.
source: Most neurons (71/98) had negative slopes, indicating stronger responses to occluded stimuli; the median slope was −0.12.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the population analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Of 216 visually responsive vlPFC neurons, 98 neurons (45%) were significantly modulated by occlusion level.
source: Of 216 neurons that were visually responsive during the test stimulus epoch (see Materials and methods), 98 neurons (45%) were significantly modulated by occlusion level (2-way ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the vlPFC neuronal population based on ANOVA analysis.

claim: Shape selectivity was stronger for occluded than unoccluded stimuli across the population of vlPFC neurons.
source: Shape selectivity was stronger for occluded than unoccluded stimuli across the population of vlPFC neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement of population-level shape selectivity analysis.

claim: For the subset of occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons, shape selectivity was strongest for occluded stimuli at intermediate occlusion levels (blue/green) and weakest for unoccluded stimuli (black).
source: For the subset of occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons, shape selectivity was strongest for occluded stimuli at intermediate occlusion levels (blue/green) and weakest for unoccluded stimuli (black) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the pattern of shape selectivity across occlusion levels shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Of 216 vlPFC neurons, the responses of 42 had a significant main effect of match/nonmatch condition.
source: Of 216 neurons, the responses of 42 had a significant main effect of match/nonmatch condition, and the responses of 65 other neurons had a significant interaction between shape and match/nonmatch condition (two-way ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of match/nonmatch effects in vlPFC neurons based on ANOVA analysis.

claim: The responses of 65 vlPFC neurons had a significant interaction between shape and match/nonmatch condition.
source: Of 216 neurons, the responses of 42 had a significant main effect of match/nonmatch condition, and the responses of 65 other neurons had a significant interaction between shape and match/nonmatch condition (two-way ANOVA, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of match/nonmatch effects in vlPFC neurons based on ANOVA analysis.

claim: In monkey cortical areas V4 and IT and in human occipitotemporal cortex, neuronal responses are strongest for unoccluded objects and neuronal shape selectivity declines gradually with increasing occlusion level.
source: In monkey cortical areas V4 (Kosai et al., 2014) and IT (Kovács et al., 1995) and in human occipitotemporal cortex (Tang et al., 2014a), neuronal responses are strongest for unoccluded objects and neuronal shape selectivity declines gradually with increasing occlusion level.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The strong responses and shape selectivity of vlPFC neurons for occluded stimuli cannot be inherited directly from visual cortex.
source: Thus, the strong responses and shape selectivity of vlPFC neurons for occluded stimuli cannot be inherited directly from visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between vlPFC and visual cortex response properties.

claim: V4 example neuron 1 had a temporal response profile with a single transient response phase (i.e. peak) followed by a sustained response phase.
source: The responses of one such example neuron (Figure 4A–B) had a temporal response profile with a single transient response phase (i.e. peak) followed by a sustained response phase.
evidence: This describes the temporal response profile of an example V4 neuron shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: V4 example neuron 2 had two transient response peaks: the first ~82 ms and the second ~150 ms after test stimulus onset.
source: The responses of one such example neuron (Figure 4C–D) had two transient response peaks: the first ~82 ms and the second ~150 ms after test stimulus onset.
evidence: This describes the timing of two response peaks for an example V4 neuron shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: For V4 example neuron 2, the neuron's responses during the first peak were strongest for the unoccluded stimulus and declined gradually with increasing occlusion level.
source: The neuron's responses during the first peak (Figure 4D, black bar) were strongest for the unoccluded stimulus and declined gradually with increasing occlusion level.
evidence: This describes the occlusion-dependence of responses during the first peak for an example V4 neuron shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For V4 example neuron 2, the neuron's responses during the second peak were strongest for intermediate occlusion levels.
source: In contrast, the neuron's responses during the second peak (Figure 4D, red bar) were strongest for intermediate occlusion levels.
evidence: This describes the occlusion-dependence of responses during the second peak for an example V4 neuron shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Of 85 V4 neurons, 30 neurons (35%; 14 neurons recorded in Monkey O and 16 neurons recorded in Monkey M) were classified as having two peaks.
source: Of 85 neurons, 30 neurons (35%; 14 neurons recorded in Monkey O and 16 neurons recorded in Monkey M) were classified as having two peaks (Figure 6A) and 55 neurons were classified as not having two peaks (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the peak-finding algorithm results applied to the V4 neuronal population.

claim: Across all V4 neurons with two peaks, the timing of the first and second peaks had a broad range, with a median of 84 ms and 214 ms, respectively.
source: Across all V4 neurons with two peaks, the timing of the first and second peaks had a broad range, with a median of 84 ms and 214 ms, respectively (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of peak timing for V4 neurons with two peaks shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Across all occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons, the peak response occurred later than in V4, 93–581 ms after test stimulus onset, with a median of 157 ms.
source: In comparison, across all occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons, the peak response occurred later than in V4, 93–581 ms after test stimulus onset, with a median of 157 ms (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of peak timing for occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The median peak time in vlPFC straddled the median peak times of the first and second response peaks in V4.
source: Thus, the median peak time in vlPFC straddled the median peak times of the first and second response peaks in V4.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the median peak times between vlPFC and V4 neurons.

claim: For V4 neurons with and without two peaks, responses during the first peak (69–99 ms) declined gradually as occlusion level increased.
source: For both groups of neurons, responses during the first peak (69–99 ms) declined gradually as occlusion level increased.
evidence: This describes the occlusion-dependence of early responses for V4 neurons.

claim: There was no significant difference between V4 neurons with and without two peaks in their responses during the first peak at any occlusion level.
source: There was no significant difference between neurons with and without two peaks in their responses during the first peak at any occlusion level (t Test, p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between two groups of V4 neurons during the first peak.

claim: For V4 neurons with two peaks, the difference in responses between the first and second peak was largest for intermediate occlusion levels and small for unoccluded stimuli and high occlusion levels.
source: For neurons with two peaks, the difference in responses between the first and second peak was largest for intermediate occlusion levels and small for unoccluded stimuli and high occlusion levels (Figure 7D, dark gray).
evidence: This describes the pattern of response differences shown in Figure 7D for V4 neurons with two peaks.

claim: The difference in responses between the first and second peaks was significantly greater for V4 neurons with two peaks than other neurons at intermediate occlusion levels.
source: The difference in responses between the first and second peaks was significantly greater for neurons with two peaks than other neurons at intermediate occlusion levels (compare curves in 7D; t Test, p<0.05, asterisks).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between V4 neurons with and without two peaks shown in Figure 7D.

claim: For unoccluded stimuli, the time course and magnitude of shape selectivity were similar for V4 neurons with and without two peaks.
source: For unoccluded stimuli (black), the time course and magnitude of shape selectivity were similar for the two neuronal groups.
evidence: This describes the comparison of shape selectivity for unoccluded stimuli between two groups of V4 neurons.

claim: For stimuli at intermediate occlusion levels (72–95% visible area), shape selectivity was stronger and reached a maximal value later for V4 neurons with two peaks.
source: For stimuli at intermediate occlusion levels (72–95% visible area), shape selectivity was stronger and reached a maximal value later for neurons with two peaks (compare corresponding colors in A and B, also see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the comparison of shape selectivity for occluded stimuli between two groups of V4 neurons shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: For V4 neurons with two peaks, shape selectivity around the time of the second peak was significantly stronger than around the time of the first peak.
source: For neurons with two peaks, shape selectivity around the time of the second peak was significantly stronger than around the time of the first peak (t Test, p<0.01; Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of shape selectivity at different time points for V4 neurons with two peaks shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The timing of maximal shape selectivity for unoccluded stimuli occurred significantly earlier than the second peak for V4 neurons with two peaks.
source: The timing of maximal shape selectivity for unoccluded stimuli occurred significantly earlier than the second peak (Figure 8D, median 131 vs. 214 ms, respectively; t Test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of timing between maximal shape selectivity and the second peak for unoccluded stimuli shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The timing of maximal shape selectivity for occluded stimuli occurred around the time of the second peak for V4 neurons with two peaks.
source: In contrast, the timing of maximal shape selectivity for occluded stimuli occurred around the time of the second peak (Figure 8E, median 188 vs. 214 ms, respectively; t Test, p>0.98),
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of timing between maximal shape selectivity and the second peak for occluded stimuli shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The enhanced shape selectivity for occluded stimuli around the time of the second peak occurred even for V4 neurons that had stronger responses during the first peak than the second peak.
source: The enhanced shape selectivity for occluded stimuli around the time of the second peak occurred even for neurons that had stronger responses during the first peak than the second peak (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes an observation about shape selectivity enhancement shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: For V4 neurons that had stronger shape selectivity during the second peak, the relative magnitude of responses during the second peak was larger for the preferred than non-preferred shapes.
source: However, for neurons that had stronger shape selectivity during the second peak, the relative magnitude of responses during the second peak was larger for the preferred than non-preferred shapes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes the relationship between response magnitude and shape selectivity shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The two-layer dynamical network model includes two V4 units and two vlPFC units.
source: The two-layer dynamical network model includes two V4 units (1 and 2) and two vlPFC units (1 and 2).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the computational model shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the model, the V4 units prefer two different shapes.
source: The V4 units prefer two different shapes.
evidence: This describes a property of the V4 units in the computational model.

claim: In the model, each vlPFC unit receives inputs from both V4 units.
source: Each vlPFC unit receives inputs from both V4 units; the shape preference of a vlPFC unit is determined by the preference of the V4 unit that provides the stronger input.
evidence: This describes the connectivity between V4 and vlPFC units in the computational model shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the model, the shape preference of a vlPFC unit is determined by the preference of the V4 unit that provides the stronger input.
source: Each vlPFC unit receives inputs from both V4 units; the shape preference of a vlPFC unit is determined by the preference of the V4 unit that provides the stronger input.
evidence: This describes how shape preference is determined for vlPFC units in the computational model.

claim: In the model, feedback inputs are passed through a rectifying nonlinearity prior to arrival in V4.
source: Feedback inputs are passed through a rectifying nonlinearity prior to arrival in V4.
evidence: This describes a processing step for feedback signals in the computational model.

claim: In the model, feedforward input to the V4 unit is strongest when the preferred shape is unoccluded and is progressively weaker for higher occlusion levels.
source: In the model, feedforward input to the V4 unit is modulated both by shape and occlusion level (Figure 10A): it is strongest when the preferred shape is unoccluded and is progressively weaker for higher occlusion levels.
evidence: This describes the properties of feedforward input to V4 units in the model shown in Figure 10A.

claim: In the model, occlusion-dependent gain modulation of feedforward input from V4 produced vlPFC unit responses that were weak to unoccluded stimuli and stronger to occluded stimuli.
source: Occlusion-dependent gain modulation of feedforward input from V4 produced vlPFC unit responses that were weak to unoccluded stimuli and stronger to occluded stimuli (Figure 10B).
evidence: This describes the output of vlPFC units in the model shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In the model, the V4 unit receiving feedback signals from vlPFC had two transient response peaks: one earlier and one later than the response peak of the vlPFC unit.
source: Furthermore, the V4 unit receiving feedback signals from vlPFC had two transient response peaks: one earlier and one later than the response peak of the vlPFC unit (Figure 10C).
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of V4 unit responses in the model shown in Figure 10C.

claim: In the model, the V4 unit's responses during the first peak were strongest for the unoccluded stimulus and declined with increasing occlusion level.
source: The V4 unit's responses during the first peak were strongest for the unoccluded stimulus and declined with increasing occlusion level.
evidence: This describes the occlusion-dependence of V4 unit responses during the first peak in the model.

claim: In the model, the V4 unit's responses during the second peak were strongest at intermediate occlusion levels.
source: In contrast, the V4 unit's responses during the second peak were strongest at intermediate occlusion levels.
evidence: This describes the occlusion-dependence of V4 unit responses during the second peak in the model.

claim: The response dynamics generated by the V4–vlPFC interaction model successfully recapitulated the dynamics observed in neuronal recordings.
source: Thus, the response dynamics generated by this V4–vlPFC interaction model successfully recapitulated the dynamics observed in our neuronal recordings (Figures 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing model simulations to experimental data.

claim: A network with only feedforward connections from V4 to vlPFC units cannot generate the second response peak in V4 units.
source: We included feedback from vlPFC to V4 because a network with only feedforward connections from V4 to vlPFC units cannot generate the second response peak in V4 units (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes a control simulation shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A demonstrating the necessity of feedback.

claim: Without synaptic adaptation on the feedforward connections from V4 to vlPFC, the feedforward-feedback loop reinforces activity in V4 and PFC units positively.
source: Second, without synaptic adaptation on the feedforward connections from V4 to vlPFC (Equation 9, Materials and methods), the feedforward-feedback loop reinforces activity in V4 and PFC units positively (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes a control simulation shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B demonstrating the necessity of synaptic adaptation.

claim: Without half-wave rectification of the feedback input from vlPFC to V4 units, the model produces a large second response peak even to presentation of non-preferred stimuli.
source: Third, without half-wave rectification of the feedback input from vlPFC to V4 units, the model produces a large second response peak even to presentation of non-preferred stimuli (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), which conflicts with the data (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes a control simulation shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2 demonstrating the necessity of half-wave rectification.

claim: When all other mechanisms are in place but the gain modulation is removed, vlPFC responses decrease with increasing occlusion level.
source: Fourth, when all other mechanisms are in place but the gain modulation is removed, vlPFC responses decrease with increasing occlusion level (Figure 10—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes a control simulation shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1C demonstrating the necessity of gain modulation.

claim: Biologically inspired models of object recognition are often implemented as hierarchical, feedforward architectures.
source: Biologically inspired models of object recognition are often implemented as hierarchical, feedforward architectures (Perrett and Oram, 1993; Wallis and Rolls, 1997; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999) despite extensive evidence for the role of feedback signaling in visual processing (Lamme et al., 1998; Gilbert and Li, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the field of computational neuroscience supported by citations.

claim: Feedforward models and artificial convolutional neural networks remain incapable of successfully recognizing partially occluded objects.
source: These feedforward models, and even more elaborate schemes such as artificial convolutional neural networks, remain incapable of successfully recognizing partially occluded objects, although they can perform other object recognition tasks well (Wyatte et al., 2012; Pepik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of computational models supported by citations.

claim: The failure of feedforward models has been attributed to the exclusion of critical computations mediated by feedback signals.
source: The failure of these models has been attributed to the exclusion of critical computations mediated by feedback signals (Yuille and Kersten, 2006; Kriegeskorte, 2015; Rust and Stocker, 2010; Tang and Kreiman, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of model failures supported by citations.

claim: More recent models that incorporate feedback signals show improved recognition performance for occluded objects.
source: Indeed, more recent models that incorporate feedback signals show improved recognition performance for occluded objects (O'Reilly et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is a statement about recent computational models supported by citations.

claim: The ventrolateral PFC (vlPFC) receives direct projections from visual cortical areas involved in higher form processing, that is V4 and inferotemporal cortex (IT).
source: However, anatomical studies demonstrate that a sub-region of PFC, the ventrolateral PFC (vlPFC), receives direct projections from visual cortical areas involved in higher form processing, that is V4 and inferotemporal cortex (IT) (Barbas and Mesulam, 1985; Ungerleider et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity supported by citations.

claim: The vlPFC sends projections back to V4 and IT.
source: The vlPFC also sends projections back to these visual areas (Ninomiya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity supported by a citation.

claim: The existence of functional interactions between vlPFC and V4 is supported by the demonstration of synchronous neural activity in the theta frequency range between lateral PFC and V4 during perceptual discrimination of visual stimuli.
source: The existence of functional interactions between these areas is also supported by the demonstration of synchronous neural activity in the theta frequency range between lateral PFC and V4 during perceptual discrimination of visual stimuli (Liebe et al., 2012) and by the engagement of PFC in perceptual processing under conditions of greater task difficulty (Jiang and Kanwisher, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about functional connectivity supported by citations.

claim: PFC is engaged in perceptual processing under conditions of greater task difficulty.
source: The existence of functional interactions between these areas is also supported by the demonstration of synchronous neural activity in the theta frequency range between lateral PFC and V4 during perceptual discrimination of visual stimuli (Liebe et al., 2012) and by the engagement of PFC in perceptual processing under conditions of greater task difficulty (Jiang and Kanwisher, 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about PFC function supported by a citation.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays an important role in cognitive control—the orchestration of thought and action in accordance with internal goals.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) plays an important role in cognitive control—the orchestration of thought and action in accordance with internal goals (Miller and Cohen, 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about PFC function supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) of monkeys performing a shape discrimination task respond more strongly to occluded than unoccluded stimuli.
source: Here, we demonstrate that neurons in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) of monkeys performing a shape discrimination task respond more strongly to occluded than unoccluded stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding from vlPFC recordings.

claim: Neurons in visual area V4 respond more strongly to unoccluded stimuli.
source: In contrast, neurons in visual area V4 respond more strongly to unoccluded stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding from V4 recordings.

claim: Many V4 neurons exhibit two transient response peaks, the second of which emerges after vlPFC response onset and displays stronger selectivity for occluded shapes.
source: Analyses of V4 response dynamics reveal that many neurons exhibit two transient response peaks, the second of which emerges after vlPFC response onset and displays stronger selectivity for occluded shapes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding from V4 response dynamics analysis.

claim: A model of V4/vlPFC interactions in which occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons feed back to shape-selective V4 neurons replicates the findings of two transient response peaks in V4.
source: We replicate these findings using a model of V4/vlPFC interactions in which occlusion-sensitive vlPFC neurons feed back to shape-selective V4 neurons, thereby enhancing V4 responses and selectivity to occluded shapes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the computational modeling results.

claim: Feedback signals from frontal and visual cortex could interact to facilitate object recognition under occlusion.
source: These results reveal how signals from frontal and visual cortex could interact to facilitate object recognition under occlusion.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Two adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) were prepared for neurophysiological recordings using sterile surgical procedures.
source: Two adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) were prepared for neurophysiological recordings using sterile surgical procedures.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: For experiments in prefrontal cortex, recording chambers were centered over the principal sulcus and targeted the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), located ventral to and along the caudal third of the principal sulcus.
source: For experiments in prefrontal cortex, recording chambers were centered over the principal sulcus and targeted the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), located ventral to and along the caudal third of the principal sulcus.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of vlPFC recordings.

claim: For experiments in visual cortex, recording chambers were centered on the dorsal surface along the prelunate gyrus and targeted area V4, extending between the lunate sulcus and the superior temporal sulcus.
source: For experiments in visual cortex, recording chambers were centered on the dorsal surface along the prelunate gyrus and targeted area V4, extending between the lunate sulcus and the superior temporal sulcus.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of V4 recordings.

claim: Recordings from V4 and vlPFC were carried out serially in the same monkeys, starting with V4 then vlPFC.
source: Recordings from the two areas were carried out serially in the same monkeys, starting with V4 then vlPFC.
evidence: This describes the temporal sequence of recordings in the two brain areas.

claim: All animal procedures conformed to NIH guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Washington.
source: All animal procedures conformed to NIH guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Washington.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the animal experiments.

claim: The results reported in the current study are based on 381 vlPFC neurons (260 and 121 from Monkey M and Monkey O, respectively) and on 85 V4 neurons (41 from Monkey M and 44 from Monkey O, respectively).
source: The results reported in the current study are based on 381 vlPFC neurons (260 and 121 from Monkey M and Monkey O, respectively) and on 85 V4 neurons (41 from Monkey M and 44 from Monkey O, respectively).
evidence: This describes the sample sizes for the neurophysiological recordings.

claim: A subset of the V4 neurons (62 of 85 neurons) contributed to a previous study.
source: A subset of the V4 neurons (62 of 85 neurons) contributed to a previous study (see Kosai et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the overlap between the current dataset and a previous publication.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented on a calibrated CRT monitor (1600 x 1200 pixels; 97 Hz frame rate; 57 cm in front of the monkey).
source: Visual stimuli were presented on a calibrated CRT monitor (1600 x 1200 pixels; 97 Hz frame rate; 57 cm in front of the monkey).
evidence: This describes the visual display equipment used in the experiments.

claim: The reference stimulus was presented for 600 ms.
source: Each stimulus was presented for 600 ms, with an inter-stimulus interval of 200 ms between the reference and the test stimuli.
evidence: This describes the timing of stimulus presentation in the behavioral task.

claim: The test stimulus was presented for 600 ms.
source: Each stimulus was presented for 600 ms, with an inter-stimulus interval of 200 ms between the reference and the test stimuli.
evidence: This describes the timing of stimulus presentation in the behavioral task.

claim: There was an inter-stimulus interval of 200 ms between the reference and the test stimuli.
source: Each stimulus was presented for 600 ms, with an inter-stimulus interval of 200 ms between the reference and the test stimuli.
evidence: This describes the timing of stimulus presentation in the behavioral task.

claim: The monkey received liquid reward for correct performance.
source: The monkey received liquid reward for correct performance.
evidence: This describes the reward contingency in the behavioral task.

claim: V4 data were collected by studying one neuron at a time and tailoring the shapes, occluding dots, colors and position of the test stimulus to the preferences of the neuron recorded.
source: V4 data were collected by studying one neuron at a time and tailoring the shapes, occluding dots, colors and position of the test stimulus to the preferences of the neuron recorded.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for V4 recordings.

claim: The vlPFC data were collected by studying several neurons simultaneously, an approach that precluded tailoring the shapes and occluding dots to the preferences of individual neurons.
source: The vlPFC data were collected by studying several neurons simultaneously, an approach that precluded tailoring the shapes and occluding dots to the preferences of individual neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for vlPFC recordings.

claim: Two shapes were used in each behavioral session, yielding four trial conditions per occlusion level (2 shapes x two behavioral outcomes).
source: Two shapes were used in each behavioral session, yielding four trial conditions per occlusion level (2 shapes x two behavioral outcomes).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for each behavioral session.

claim: In V4 recordings, 4–9 occlusion levels were sampled (median = 6).
source: In V4 recordings, we sampled 4–9 oc clusion levels (median = 6).
evidence: This describes the number of occlusion levels tested in V4 recordings.

claim: In vlPFC recordings, 5–6 occlusion levels were sampled (median = 5).
source: In vlPFC recordings, we sampled 5–6 oc clusion levels (median = 5).
evidence: This describes the number of occlusion levels tested in vlPFC recordings.

claim: Only data from neurons tested with at least seven repeated presentations of each trial condition and of each occlusion level tested were included.
source: We only included data from neurons tested with at least seven repeated presentations of each trial condition and of each occlusion level tested.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for neurons in the analysis.

claim: The median number of repeats was 24 for V4 recordings and 15 for vlPFC recordings.
source: The median number of repeats was 24 for V4 recordings and 15 for vlPFC recordings.
evidence: This describes the number of trial repetitions for V4 and vlPFC recordings.

claim: Among 381 vlPFC neurons, 216 (142/260 in Monkey M and 74/121 in Monkey O) were significantly responsive during the test stimulus epoch (t Test, p<0.01).
source: Among 381 vlPFC neurons, 216 (142/260 in Monkey M and 74/121 in Monkey O) were significantly responsive during the test stimulus epoch (t Test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of visually responsive vlPFC neurons.

claim: Among the 216 visually responsive vlPFC neurons, the responses of 66 neurons showed a significant dependence on stimulus shape (p<0.05).
source: Among the 216 visually responsive neurons, the responses of 98 neurons (71/260 in Monkey M and 27/121 in Monkey O) showed a significant dependence on occlusion level (p<0.05) and the responses of 66 neurons showed a significant dependence on stimulus shape (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of shape-selective vlPFC neurons based on ANOVA analysis.

claim: Shape selectivity values ranged from 0.5 (unselective) to 1.0 (very selective).
source: Shape selectivity values ranged from 0.5 (unselective) to 1.0 (very selective).
evidence: This describes the range of shape selectivity values computed using ROC analysis.

claim: Of 85 V4 neurons, 43 had no robust peaks beyond the first transient that passed the peak amplitude and modulation criteria.
source: Of 85 V4 neurons, 43 had no robust peaks beyond the first transient that passed the peak amplitude and modulation criteria.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the peak-finding algorithm results.

claim: Of the remaining 42 V4 neurons, 30 had a second peak that showed a statistically significant response increase relative to the preceding trough.
source: Of the remaining 42 neurons, 30 had a second peak that showed a statistically significant response increase relative to the preceding trough; these neurons were classified as having two peaks.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the peak-finding algorithm results with statistical testing.

claim: 29/30 V4 neurons had exactly one peak that qualified as the second response peak.
source: Specifically, 29/30 neuons had exactly one peak that qualified as the second response peak.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the number of second peaks identified per neuron.

claim: The model includes feedback from vlPFC to V4, synaptic adaptation in the feedforward inputs from V4 to vlPFC, half-wave rectification of feedback signals from vlPFC to V4, and occlusion-dependent gain modulation input to vlPFC.
source: We started with the simplest feedforward model composed of two V4 units and two vlPFC units, and we included four mechanisms to achieve the desired dynamics in V4 and vlPFC responses: (1) feedback from vlPFC to V4; (2) synaptic adaptation in the feedforward inputs from V4 to vlPFC; (3) half-wave rectification of feedback signals from vlPFC to V4; (4) occlusion-dependent gain modulation input to vlPFC.
evidence: This describes the key mechanisms included in the computational model.

claim: Feedback from vlPFC to V4 is necessary to reproduce the response dynamics observed in V4.
source: Thus, in our model, feedback from vlPFC to V4 is necessary to reproduce the response dynamics observed in V4.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control simulations testing the necessity of feedback.

claim: Without half-wave rectification, the enhanced shape selectivity during the second peak in the V4 neuronal data is not reproduced by the model.
source: Thus, without half-wave rectification, the enhanced shape selectivity during the second peak in the V4 neuronal data (Figure 8C) is not reproduced by the model.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control simulations testing the necessity of half-wave rectification.

claim: Anatomical observations of disynaptic feedback connections between V4 and vlPFC exist.
source: Indeed, anatomical observations of disynaptic feedback connections between V4 and vlPFC exist (Ninomiya et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical connectivity supported by a citation.

claim: The model simulations were unaffected by delays of up to ~50 ms in the arrival of gain modulation relative to the arrival of shape selective signals.
source: To consider the possibility that gain modulation of vlPFC may be mediated by signals from V4 or IT cortex, we verified that our simulations were unaffected by delays of up to ~50 ms in the arrival of gain modulation relative to the arrival of shape selective signals (Figure 10—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes control simulations testing the effect of delays in gain modulation shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: Visual representations in vlPFC do not always mirror representations in visual cortex.
source: Our results demonstrate that visual representations in vlPFC do not always mirror representations in visual cortex and suggest that vlPFC may play an important role in representing objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings comparing vlPFC and V4 responses.

claim: vlPFC may play an important role in representing objects.
source: Our results demonstrate that visual representations in vlPFC do not always mirror representations in visual cortex and suggest that vlPFC may play an important role in representing objects.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The preference for occluded stimuli in vlPFC was independent of dot color.
source: We verified in control experiments that the preference for occluded stimuli was independent of dot color (data not shown).
evidence: This describes control experiments that were conducted but not shown in detail.

claim: vlPFC neuronal responses were weaker when the occluding dots were in the same color as the background.
source: We also verified in control experiments that vlPFC neuronal responses were weaker when the occluding dots were in the same color as the background – an observation suggesting that the vlPFC responses we observed rely on explicit occlusion-related signals.
evidence: This describes control experiments that were conducted but not shown in detail.

claim: vlPFC responses arise from the modulation of occlusion-dependent, shape-selective feedforward signals from V4 by another feedforward signal that is dependent only on the occlusion level.
source: We propose that vlPFC responses arise from the modulation of occlusion-dependent, shape-selective feedforward signals from V4 by another feedforward signal that is dependent only on the occlusion level.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for how vlPFC responses are generated.

claim: The responses of many IT neurons were consistent with encoding the total area of the occluders.
source: Indeed, in one monkey performing the same behavioral task used in the current study, we found that the responses of many IT neurons were consistent with encoding the total area of the occluders (Namima and Pasupathy, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about IT neuron responses supported by a citation.

claim: The comparison of reference and test stimuli is unlikely to be implemented in vlPFC.
source: Our results suggest, however, that the comparison of reference and test stimuli is unlikely to be implemented in vlPFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of vlPFC responses.

claim: If behavioral performance depended on comparisons implemented in vlPFC, discriminability would be higher for occluded stimuli and lower for unoccluded stimuli – the opposite of the performance observed.
source: We found stronger neuronal selectivity in vlPFC for occluded than unoccluded test stimuli. Thus, if behavioral performance depended on comparisons implemented in vlPFC, discriminability would be higher for occluded stimuli and lower for unoccluded stimuli – the opposite of the performance we observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on comparing neuronal selectivity to behavioral performance.

claim: The weak neuronal responses in vlPFC to unoccluded stimuli are consistent with a report of weak neuronal selectivity in this area for stimulus color in monkeys performing a color change detection task.
source: The weak neuronal responses in vlPFC to unoccluded stimuli are consistent with a report of weak neuronal selectivity in this area for stimulus color in monkeys performing a color change detection task (Lara and Wallis, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from another study supported by a citation.

claim: These findings challenge the notion that vlPFC activity mediates perceptual discriminations of form and color directly.
source: Together, these findings challenge the notion that vlPFC activity mediates perceptual discriminations of form and color directly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous work.

claim: The comparison of sensory representations could be implemented in other parts of the PFC or in sensory cortex, where signals correlated with monkeys' behavioral decisions have been reported.
source: The comparison of sensory representations could be implemented in other parts of the PFC or in sensory cortex, where signals correlated with monkeys' behavioral decisions have been reported (Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Eskandar et al., 1992; Miller and Desimone, 1994; Wallis and Miller, 2003; Romo and Salinas, 2003; Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006; Kosai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative locations for decision-related computations supported by citations.

claim: The evidence for functional connectivity between V4 and lateral PFC during memory maintenance supports the implementation of decision computations in visual cortex.
source: The evidence for functional connectivity between V4 and lateral PFC during memory maintenance also supports the implementation of decision computations in visual cortex (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about functional connectivity supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that the vlPFC responses reflect this area's engagement in facilitating decisions under limited sensory evidence.
source: Given that the monkeys were required to report their perceptual judgments, it is possible that the vlPFC responses we recorded reflect this area's engagement in facilitating decisions under limited sensory evidence.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the vlPFC responses.

claim: When shape selectivity in visual cortex is weakened by the presence of occlusion, decision-making becomes difficult.
source: When shape selectivity in visual cortex is weakened by the presence of occlusion (Kosai et al., 2014; Kovács et al., 1995; Tang et al., 2014a), decision-making becomes difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between visual cortex responses and decision-making supported by citations.

claim: vlPFC feedback might serve to amplify weak signals expressly to facilitate decisions.
source: In this case, vlPFC feedback might serve to amplify weak signals expressly to facilitate decisions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of vlPFC feedback.

claim: The results are consistent with vlPFC's engagement in tasks of greater difficulty or cognitive demand.
source: In this regard, our results are consistent with vlPFC's engagement in tasks of greater difficulty or cognitive demand (Crittenden and Duncan, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from another study supported by a citation.

claim: When the task becomes difficult, rather than reflecting task difficulty per se, vlPFC responses amplify behaviorally relevant signals to facilitate perceptual decisions.
source: Importantly, when the task becomes difficult, rather than reflecting task difficulty per se, we propose that vlPFC responses amplify behaviorally relevant signals to facilitate perceptual decisions.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the role of vlPFC responses.

claim: The preference of vlPFC neurons for occluded stimuli may be related to the specific engagement of vlPFC in the recognition of occluded objects.
source: An alternative possibility is that the preference of vlPFC neurons for occluded stimuli may be related to the specific engagement of vlPFC in the recognition of occluded objects.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the vlPFC responses.

claim: The processing of complex visual scenes containing clutter and occlusions may be guided by higher cognitive, memory processes.
source: Previous work has argued that the processing of complex visual scenes containing clutter and occlusions may be guided by higher cognitive, memory processes (Cavanagh, 1991; Kveraga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about visual processing supported by citations.

claim: Image representations in early and mid-level areas of the ventral visual pathway may be relayed to higher processing stages where they are compared to stored representations of object prototypes, leading to the recognition of objects in the scene.
source: For example, image representations in early and mid-level areas of the ventral visual pathway may be relayed to higher processing stages where they are compared to stored representations of object prototypes, leading to the recognition of objects in the scene (Kveraga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about a proposed mechanism for object recognition supported by a citation.

claim: This recognition process may then guide the grouping of appropriate contours and regions, thereby facilitating object segmentation and scene understanding.
source: This recognition process may then guide the grouping of appropriate contours and regions, thereby facilitating object segmentation and scene understanding (McDermott, 2004; Kveraga et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about a proposed mechanism for scene understanding supported by citations.

claim: The results are broadly consistent with the possibility that vlPFC activity embodies a recognition signal that is fed back to V4 to refine object representations.
source: Our results are also broadly consistent with the possibility that vlPFC activity embodies a recognition signal that is fed back to V4 to refine object representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of vlPFC activity.

claim: Studies of object representation and recognition often consider spiking activity only within the first hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset.
source: Studies of object representation and recognition often consider spiking activity only within the first hundred milliseconds after stimulus onset (e.g. Hung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about common practices in the field supported by a citation.

claim: The rationale for choosing the early temporal epoch for analysis is based on the argument that successful categorization can be achieved by feedforward processes alone.
source: The rationale for choosing this early temporal epoch for analysis is based on the argument that successful categorization can be achieved by feedforward processes alone (VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001; Serre et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for focusing on early responses supported by citations.

claim: Neuronal responses to visual stimuli depend not only on signals carried by feedforward connections but also by feedback and horizontal connections.
source: However, neuronal responses to visual stimuli depend not only on signals carried by feedforward connections but also by feedback and horizontal connections.
evidence: This is a statement about the factors influencing neuronal responses.

claim: Feedback and horizontal connections may modulate neuronal responses based on stimulus context and behavioral goals, and confer selectivity for more complex visual stimuli.
source: Feedback and horizontal connections may modulate neuronal responses based on stimulus context and behavioral goals, and confer selectivity for more complex visual stimuli (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000; Gilbert and Li, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the role of feedback and horizontal connections supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies comparing V4 and V1 response dynamics during contour grouping and scene segmentation tasks suggest that feedback from V4 to V1 enhances the representation of figures and suppresses the representation of backgrounds in V1.
source: For example, recent studies comparing V4 and V1 response dynamics during contour grouping and scene segmentation tasks suggest that feedback from V4 to V1 enhances the representation of figures and suppresses the representation of backgrounds in V1 (Chen et al., 2014; Poort et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from other studies supported by citations.

claim: Feedback from vlPFC to V4 enhances the representation of behaviorally relevant, occluded shapes in V4.
source: Similarly, our results suggest that feedback from vlPFC to V4 enhances the representation of behaviorally relevant, occluded shapes in V4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on comparison to other studies.

claim: The model simulations suggest that the enhancement of V4 shape selectivity could be mediated even by weakly tuned vlPFC neurons.
source: Our model simulations suggest that the enhancement of V4 shape selectivity could be mediated even by weakly tuned vlPFC neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling results.

claim: IT recordings suggest that putative feedback from IT may not be well-suited for enhancing V4 shape selectivity at intermediate occlusion levels.
source: However, our IT recordings suggest this is unlikely because, as in V4, shape selectivity in IT is stronger for unoccluded than occluded stimuli (Namima and Pasupathy, 2016). Thus, putative feedback from IT may not be well-suited for enhancing V4 shape selectivity at intermediate occlusion levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on IT recording data cited from another study.

claim: The diversity in timing of the second peak is likely because V4 and vlPFC are connected via feedforward and feedback pathways that are direct and indirect, and these different pathways are expected to have different conduction times.
source: The diversity in timing of the second peak is likely because V4 and vlPFC are connected via feedforward and feedback pathways that are direct and indirect, and these different pathways are expected to have different conduction times.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the variability in second peak timing.

claim: It is possible that feedback signals from vlPFC to V4 are carried by a sparse projection and then distributed more broadly across V4 via horizontal connections, resulting in longer delays between the peak of vlPFC responses and the second peak of V4 responses.
source: It is also possible that feedback signals from vlPFC to V4 are carried by a sparse projection and then distributed more broadly across V4 via horizontal connections, resulting in longer delays (than expected for disynaptic transmission) between the peak of vlPFC responses and the second peak of V4 responses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the delays between vlPFC and V4 response peaks.

claim: The strength of connections between V4 and vlPFC is likely heterogeneous, which could explain the range of second peak magnitudes documented.
source: The strength of connections between V4 and vlPFC is likely heterogeneous, which could explain the range of second peak magnitudes we documented.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the variability in second peak magnitude.

claim: The model simulations demonstrate that even weak functional interactions between V4 and vlPFC could result in a small, second response peak in V4 that may be undetectable in highly variable responses.
source: Our simulations demonstrate that even weak functional interactions between the two areas could result in a small, second response peak in V4 that may be undetectable in highly variable responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling results.

claim: The heterogeneous properties of the second response peak support the possibility that V4 neurons with and without two peaks lie along a continuum.
source: Overall, the heterogeneous properties of the second response peak support the possibility that V4 neurons with and without two peaks lie along a continuum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the heterogeneity observed in V4 responses.

claim: V4 and vlPFC recordings were conducted in separate sessions so individual trial comparisons of V4 and vlPFC activity cannot be made.
source: First, we conducted V4 and vlPFC recordings in separate sessions so we cannot compare V4 and vlPFC activity on individual trials.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: Only two discriminanda were used in each behavioral session, so it is not known whether vlPFC neurons are sufficiently sensitive to shape information to mediate the recognition of occluded objects.
source: Second, we used only two discriminanda in each behavioral session, so we do not know whether vlPFC neurons are sufficiently sensitive to shape information to mediate the recognition of occluded objects.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Monkeys were not instructed to report their behavioral decisions as soon as possible, so the precise epoch of V4 neural activity that mediates perceptual judgments cannot be inferred.
source: Third, we did not instruct monkeys to report their behavioral decisions as soon as possible, so we cannot infer the precise epoch of V4 neural activity that mediates perceptual judgments.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the behavioral task design.

claim: It is not known whether V4 neuronal responses during the second transient peak, which have stronger shape selectivity, contributed to the monkeys' perceptual decisions.
source: Specifically, we do not know whether V4 neuronal responses during the second transient peak, which have stronger shape selectivity, contributed to the monkeys' perceptual decisions.
evidence: This describes a limitation in interpreting the functional significance of the second peak.

claim: It is not known whether the engagement of vlPFC neurons was contingent on the monkeys reporting their perceptual decisions, or whether these same neurons would also be engaged in the recognition of partially occluded objects in natural viewing conditions.
source: Fourth, we do not know whether the engagement of vlPFC neurons in our study was contingent on the monkeys reporting their perceptual decisions, or whether these same neurons would also be engaged in the recognition of partially occluded objects in natural viewing conditions.
evidence: This describes a limitation in understanding the generalizability of the vlPFC responses.

claim: Partial occlusions pose a major challenge to the successful recognition of visual objects because they reduce the evidence available to the brain.
source: Partial occlusions pose a major challenge to the successful recognition of visual objects because they reduce the evidence available to the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenge posed by occlusion.

claim: Recognizing partially occluded objects could require solving an ill-posed inverse problem, one that lacks a unique solution because the retinal image of an occluded object is often compatible with multiple interpretations.
source: Recognizing partially occluded objects could require solving an ill-posed inverse problem (Helmholtz, 1910; Yuille and Kersten, 2006), one that lacks a unique solution because the retinal image of an occluded object is often compatible with multiple interpretations (e.g. see Bregman's B illusion, Bregman, 1981).
evidence: This is a statement about the computational challenge of recognizing occluded objects supported by citations.

claim: Recognition must rely not only on information about the physical object but also on information about the occlusion, scene context and perceptual experience.
source: As a result, recognition must rely not only on information about the physical object but also on information about the occlusion, scene context and perceptual experience.
evidence: This is a statement about the information required for recognizing occluded objects.

claim: The results provide support for the hypothesis that feedback signals from vlPFC, which carry information about occlusions, contribute to object representation in V4 and to object recognition under occlusion.
source: Our results provide support for the hypothesis that feedback signals from vlPFC, which carry information about occlusions, contribute to object representation in V4 and to object recognition under occlusion.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Other brain regions, for example IT cortex, are likely to be involved in object recognition under occlusion and should be studied.
source: Other brain regions, for example IT cortex, are likely to be involved and should be studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.
